questions.q: Which climate does Pinot Noir need to make good-quality wine?
questions.ex: Pinot Noir is thin-skinned and prone to rot. Where it is too warm the fruit tastes cooked rather than fresh.

questions.q: Which description best fits a typical Pinot Noir?
o: Pale to medium colour, high acidity, low to medium tannins, red fruit
Deep colour, high acidity, high tannins, blackcurrant
Deep colour, medium acidity, medium tannins, black plum
Pale colour, low acidity, high tannins, black pepper
questions.ex: Pinot Noir is usually pale to medium in colour with high acidity, low to medium tannins and red fruit such as strawberry, raspberry and red cherry.

questions.q: Why do many Pinot Noir producers prefer older or larger oak barrels?
o: Strong flavours from small new barrels can swamp Pinot Noir's delicate fruit
Older barrels add more tannin to a thin-skinned grape
Burgundy's rules ban new oak for red wine
questions.ex: Older and larger barrels give less oak flavour. The best Pinot Noirs show only subtle oak (smoke, cloves) balanced by fruit.

questions.q: Which of these Burgundy village appellations is in the Côte de Nuits?
questions.ex: Gevrey-Chambertin and Nuits-Saint-Georges are in the Côte de Nuits (the northern half of the Côte d'Or). Beaune and Pommard are in the Côte de Beaune, as is Meursault.

questions.q: On a red Burgundy label, which term indicates the highest category of vineyard?
questions.ex: The hierarchy runs Bourgogne (regional), then village appellations, then Premier Cru vineyards, with Grand Cru vineyards at the top.

questions.q: A very good red Burgundy has been ageing in bottle for many years. Which tertiary aromas would you expect?
questions.ex: Top Pinot Noir develops forest floor and mushroom in bottle. Petrol and honey are typical of aged Riesling; vanilla and coconut come from new oak.

questions.q: Which New Zealand region makes the country's ripest, most powerful Pinot Noir, protected by a ring of mountains?
questions.ex: Central Otago has very sunny days and cool nights, giving pronounced strawberry and red cherry fruit, medium to full body and medium tannins.

questions.q: What keeps Los Carneros (Carneros) cool enough for high-quality Pinot Noir and Chardonnay?
o: Morning fog from San Pablo Bay
questions.ex: Carneros is cooled by morning fogs rolling in from San Pablo Bay. The western parts of Sonoma are cooled by Pacific breezes instead.

questions.q: Which pair of Australian regions is cool enough for Pinot Noir, thanks to breezes from the Southern Ocean?
questions.ex: Both are in Victoria. Their Pinot Noir ranges from light and fragrant to riper wines with cooked red fruit.

questions.q: Which Chilean region is best known for Pinot Noir, thanks to sea breezes and morning fog?
questions.ex: Casablanca Valley is coastal, north of Santiago. Its Pinot Noir is very fruity, often with cooked strawberry, and can be good value.

questions.q: Walker Bay, cooled by strong southerly sea breezes, has a reputation for which black grape?
questions.ex: South Africa's Pinot Noir is focused on its coolest coastal regions such as Walker Bay, where it gives vibrant red fruit.

questions.q: What levels of acidity and tannin are typical of a single-varietal Merlot?
questions.ex: Merlot is typically dry with medium acidity and medium tannins, which is why it softens blends with higher-tannin grapes.

questions.q: Merlot picked when only just ripe gives which flavours?
o: Red fruit (strawberry, red plum) and green bell pepper
questions.ex: Just-ripe Merlot is light to medium-bodied with red fruit and herbaceous notes. Riper Merlot moves to cooked black fruit and fuller body.

questions.q: Why is Merlot often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon?
o: It adds red fruit and lowers the tannin, so the wine is ready to drink sooner
It adds acidity to a low-acid grape
It adds colour and tannin to a pale grape
questions.ex: Cabernet Sauvignon is high in tannin. Merlot softens the blend and adds red-fruit flavours.

questions.q: Which Bordeaux appellations are most famous for Merlot-dominated wines?
questions.ex: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol are on the Right Bank, where Merlot is the most important grape. The others are Left Bank, where Cabernet Sauvignon usually dominates.

questions.q: How does Bordeaux Supérieur AOC differ from Bordeaux AOC?
o: Slightly stricter rules on yields, ageing and minimum alcohol
It can only come from the Left Bank
It is only made by classified châteaux
questions.ex: Both can come from anywhere in Bordeaux. Bordeaux Supérieur has slightly stricter rules.

questions.q: Where does most of New Zealand's Merlot come from?
questions.ex: Hawke's Bay, on the North Island, has a moderate climate with plentiful rain. Its Merlot ranges from light and fruity to full-bodied.

questions.q: Chile's warm, dry Central Valley is especially important for which kind of Merlot?
o: Soft, medium-bodied wines for high-volume brands
Light, high-acid wines for sparkling base
Long-aged wines from old vines on steep slopes
questions.ex: Merlot ripens easily there with high yields. Altitude allows some fresher styles too.

questions.q: As the best Merlot-dominated wines age in bottle, which notes develop?
questions.ex: Top Right Bank Merlot ages well, developing dried fruit and tobacco.

questions.q: Which best describes the climate of Bordeaux?
o: Moderate, with high rainfall from the nearby Atlantic
Warm and dry, sheltered by mountains
Cool, with frequent spring frost and little rain
questions.ex: Bordeaux's variable weather is why blending matters so much: the Merlot share rises in years when Cabernet Sauvignon struggles to ripen.

questions.q: Which description best fits a typical Cabernet Sauvignon?
o: Deep colour, high acidity, high tannins, blackcurrant and mint or green bell pepper
Pale colour, high acidity, low tannins, strawberry
Medium colour, medium acidity, medium tannins, red plum
Deep colour, low acidity, low tannins, black pepper
questions.ex: Its thick skins give deep colour and high tannin. Black fruit with herbal or herbaceous notes is the signature.

questions.q: Why can Cabernet Sauvignon struggle to ripen in many parts of Bordeaux?
o: Its thick skins need a long, warm growing season
Its thin skins rot easily in the rain
It ripens so early that acidity is lost
It needs frozen grapes to concentrate sugar
questions.ex: It grows in moderate and warm climates, but in moderate climates only the warmest sites ripen it reliably.

questions.q: How do the gravel soils of Bordeaux's Left Bank help Cabernet Sauvignon ripen?
o: They drain rain away quickly and store heat that warms the vines at night
They hold water through dry summers
They are rich in nutrients that boost yields
They reflect sunlight off the Gironde estuary
questions.ex: The stones keep the roots from staying cold and wet, and release the day's heat after dark.

questions.q: Why is young Cabernet Sauvignon often matured in oak barrels?
o: Small amounts of oxygen through the wood soften its tannins
questions.ex: New oak also adds smoke, vanilla and cloves.

questions.q: Which sub-region in the far north of the Napa Valley is warmest and gives some of its ripest, fullest Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.ex: Oakville and Rutherford also make full-bodied, ripe Cabernet. Carneros is cool and better known for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

questions.q: A South Australian Cabernet Sauvignon shows mint, pronounced blackcurrant and cedar from oak. Where is it most likely from?
questions.ex: Coonawarra is moderated by cloud cover and cool southerly breezes. Its Cabernet is typically very good to outstanding and ages well.

questions.q: What does Cru Bourgeois on a Bordeaux label indicate?
o: A Médoc wine outside the Grand Cru Classé ranking that may use this term
A wine made from bought-in grapes
Basic Bordeaux AOC with extra bottle age
questions.ex: Most Cru Bourgeois wines cost less than classified châteaux, though some are very good to outstanding.

questions.q: What does Château on a Bordeaux label tell you?
o: The wine was made from grapes grown on the producer's own land
The wine is a Grand Cru Classé
The wine was matured in new oak
questions.ex: It refers to an estate or producer, not necessarily a grand building.

questions.q: Which two sub-regions of Chile's Central Valley are especially important for Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.ex: They run from the Andes foothills to the Coastal Ranges. Foothill wines often show mint and green bell pepper. Cabernet is Chile's most planted variety.

questions.q: Which of these is a Left Bank appellation where Cabernet Sauvignon usually dominates?
questions.ex: Pauillac and Margaux are inside the Haut-Médoc. Pessac-Léognan, within Graves, is also Left Bank.

questions.q: What does Grand Cru Classé or Cru Classé on a Bordeaux label mean?
o: The wine comes from a château ranked in one of Bordeaux's classifications
The vineyard is a Burgundy-style single grand cru plot
The wine has been aged for at least ten years
The grapes were affected by noble rot
questions.ex: Some of the classifications are old, but they are still seen as a strong sign of quality, and the wines can age for decades.

questions.q: Which aroma is most characteristic of Syrah/Shiraz?
questions.ex: Black fruit with black pepper is the classic Syrah/Shiraz profile. Green bell pepper suggests Cabernet Sauvignon or Sauvignon Blanc.

questions.q: Compared with a Northern Rhône Syrah, a warm-climate Barossa Valley Shiraz is more likely to be:
o: Full-bodied and high in alcohol, with cooked black fruit and liquorice
Higher in acidity with herbal notes
questions.ex: Moderate-climate Syrah is medium-bodied with fresh black fruit, herbs and pepper. Warm-climate Shiraz is riper and fuller.

questions.q: In Côte-Rôtie, some producers ferment a small amount of which white grape with their Syrah?
questions.ex: Co-fermenting a little Viognier can add floral aromas. Not every producer does it.

questions.q: How does Crozes-Hermitage generally compare with Hermitage?
o: A larger, flatter area making less intense wines that usually cost less
A single steep south-facing hill with the most intense wines
A sweet red style made from dried grapes
A white wine appellation for Viognier
questions.ex: Crozes-Hermitage surrounds the hill of Hermitage. Higher yields and machine-friendly vineyards keep prices lower.

questions.q: Which describes a typical Hunter Valley Shiraz?
o: Medium-bodied with fresh black fruit, developing earth and meat with age
Full-bodied with cooked black fruit and very high alcohol
Light and sweet with red fruit
Pale and low in tannin with strawberry
questions.ex: The Hunter Valley is warm, but summer cloud and sea breezes slow ripening.

questions.q: A Shiraz labelled South Eastern Australia is most likely to be:
o: An inexpensive high-volume wine from warm inland regions
A wine from very old Barossa Valley vines
A single-vineyard wine from a cool coastal site
questions.ex: Shiraz is Australia's most planted grape, and much of it grows in warm inland areas for brands labelled South Eastern Australia.

questions.q: Syrah is blended into the wines of which South of France appellation?
questions.ex: In the warm South of France Syrah ripens reliably. It is also found as single-varietal Pays d'Oc IGP.

questions.q: As the finest Syrah/Shiraz ages in bottle, which flavours emerge?
o: Dried fruit, leather, meat and earth
questions.ex: Ageing can run to a decade or more for the best wines.

questions.q: In the Northern Rhône, what is the position of Syrah in the AOC wines?
o: It is the only black grape permitted
It must be blended with Grenache
It is a minor blending partner to Mourvèdre
It is only used for rosé
questions.ex: The steep slopes need hand work, which makes the wines expensive to produce.

questions.q: A dry white with high acidity, light body and flavours of apple, lemon and wet stones is most likely a Chardonnay from a:
questions.ex: Cool-climate Chardonnay is high in acidity with green fruit, citrus and wet stones.

questions.q: A full-bodied Chardonnay with medium acidity and flavours of peach, pineapple and banana is most likely from a:
questions.ex: Warm-climate Chardonnay is full-bodied and dominated by stone and tropical fruit.

questions.q: Which winemaking option gives Chardonnay buttery, creamy flavours and softens its acidity?
questions.ex: Lees contact adds bread and biscuit plus body. New oak adds smoke, vanilla and coconut.

questions.q: Which best describes a typical Chablis?
o: Dry, high acidity, apple, lemon and wet stones, usually with no oak flavour
Full-bodied with tropical fruit and strong vanilla
questions.ex: Chablis is cool. Producers usually ferment in inert vessels to keep the delicate fruit. Frost is a key risk.

questions.q: Which two Côte de Beaune villages are famous for Chardonnay?
questions.ex: Their wines are often fermented or matured in oak with lees contact, and the best age for decades (hazelnut, mushroom).

questions.q: Where is Pouilly-Fuissé?
questions.ex: Don't confuse it with Pouilly-Fumé (Loire Sauvignon Blanc). Pouilly-Fuissé is Chardonnay from sun-trap slopes, often oaked.

questions.q: A Chardonnay labelled simply California, with peach and pineapple and a hint of oak, most likely comes from:
o: Warm, irrigated Central Valley vineyards, with oak from chips or staves
Fog-cooled vineyards in Carneros, aged in new barrels
Single vineyards in Santa Barbara County
High-altitude sites in the Sierra Nevada
questions.ex: The Central Valley is cut off from the sea by mountains. High yields go into high-volume brands without a GI.

questions.q: What mainly cools the Adelaide Hills?
questions.ex: Adelaide Hills is cooled by altitude; the Yarra Valley by ocean currents from the south. Both make Chardonnay with ripe peach and medium to high acidity.

questions.q: Chardonnay is the most widely planted white grape in which moderate-climate New Zealand region?
questions.ex: Hawke's Bay Chardonnay is full-bodied, with high acidity and pronounced stone fruit.

questions.q: Which tertiary flavours does a top Chardonnay develop after years in bottle?
questions.ex: Very good or outstanding Chardonnay can age for years or decades.

questions.q: Why do winemakers often add acid to warm-climate Chardonnay?
o: To balance its alcohol and body
questions.ex: Warm climates leave grapes low in acid. Acidification is common there.

questions.q: Which aromas are most typical of Sauvignon Blanc?
o: Grass, green bell pepper and asparagus
questions.ex: Sauvignon Blanc is aromatic and herbaceous, usually dry and high in acidity.

questions.q: When is most Sauvignon Blanc best drunk?
o: Young, within a year or two of the vintage
questions.ex: Even outstanding examples can lose their fresh aromas within a couple of years and turn vegetal.

questions.q: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé are Sauvignon Blancs from which French region?
questions.ex: They face each other across the Loire. The climate is cool, giving apple, grass, asparagus and sometimes wet stones.

questions.q: Compared with Sancerre, a typical Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is:
o: More pronounced, with fruit from lemon to passion fruit and strong green bell pepper
questions.ex: Marlborough producers often blend grapes from different sites and ripeness levels, which widens the flavour range.

questions.q: In Graves and Pessac-Léognan, Sauvignon Blanc is usually blended with which grape?
questions.ex: Sémillon adds body and helps the wine age. The best are often oaked and develop honey and nuts.

questions.q: Which South African region is cooled by altitude and often called the country's coolest?
questions.ex: Elgin's Sauvignon Blanc shows green apple and sometimes wet stones. Constantia is cooled by sea breezes instead.

questions.q: A Sauvignon Blanc labelled Touraine AOC is typically:
questions.ex: Touraine is a wide area west of Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé.

questions.q: How do Napa Valley producers make fresh, herbaceous Sauvignon Blanc in a mostly warm state?
o: Using cooler sites and picking early
Leaving the grapes to raisin on the vine
questions.ex: Early picking keeps the acidity and herbaceous aromas. Some are made with oak for body and smoke.

questions.q: If a Sauvignon Blanc has seen oak, which label term often signals it?
questions.ex: Most single-varietal Sauvignon Blanc is made in inert vessels, because new oak can overwhelm its herbaceous character.

questions.q: Why is Riesling usually fermented in stainless steel or other inert vessels?
o: To preserve its floral and fruity aromas
Because oak raises its acidity too far
questions.ex: Riesling is aromatic. Oak or buttery flavours would hide its character.

questions.q: Which aromas develop as a fine Riesling ages in bottle?
questions.ex: High acidity keeps the wine fresh for years or decades while these tertiary notes develop.

questions.q: Compared with Rieslings from further south in Germany, a typical Mosel Riesling is:
o: Lighter-bodied and often medium-sweet, with very high acidity
questions.ex: The Mosel is far north. The best vineyards are steep slopes above the river, helped by stony soils and reflected sunlight.

questions.q: Which German region, sheltered by mountains to the west, makes Riesling that is typically dry and medium-bodied, much like Alsace?
questions.ex: The Pfalz is dry and sunny with a long growing season. Rheingau Riesling is drier and fuller than Mosel, from south-facing slopes on the Rhine.

questions.q: Why can Australia's Clare Valley and Eden Valley make fresh, dry Riesling?
o: Their higher altitude gives a moderate climate
They are as far south as New Zealand
questions.ex: Their Riesling is dry with pronounced lime, peach, blossom and petrol. The nearby Barossa Valley is warm.

questions.q: Why is Alsace one of France's driest and sunniest regions?
o: The Vosges Mountains block rain-bearing westerly winds
It is close to the Mediterranean
Fog burns off early every day
Its vineyards are at very high altitude
questions.ex: Long sunny autumns let grapes ripen slowly. Alsace Riesling is typically dry, medium-bodied and high in acidity.

questions.q: Which Prädikat level requires the least sugar in the grapes?
questions.ex: Kabinett is the lightest, most delicate Prädikat. Spätlese and then Auslese need riper grapes.

questions.q: Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) is made from:
o: Individually selected berries shrivelled by noble rot
questions.ex: TBA is rare and very concentrated, like a more intense Beerenauslese. Frozen grapes make Eiswein; selected bunches make Auslese.

questions.q: Which statement about Eiswein is true?
o: It is made from grapes frozen on the vine, and botrytis plays no part
It is made from botrytis-affected grapes
It can be made every year in Germany
questions.ex: The weather needed doesn't happen every year, yields are tiny and the wines are expensive.

questions.q: If each is made in a dry (trocken) style, which would have the highest alcohol?
questions.ex: A higher Prädikat needs more sugar in the grapes, so a dry version ferments to more alcohol.

questions.q: What does Halbtrocken on a German label mean?
questions.ex: Trocken means dry. These terms clarify sweetness when the Prädikat alone could be ambiguous.

questions.q: Which German term means a PDO wine from one of 13 regions, with a lower ripeness requirement than Prädikatswein?
questions.ex: Landwein is the German PGI term. Prädikatswein needs riper grapes from a single region.

questions.q: Besides stopping fermentation by removing the yeast, how are some off-dry or medium Rieslings made?
o: Adding sterile grape juice (Süssreserve) to a dry wine
questions.ex: The sweetest styles use extra-ripe grapes so sweet that fermentation stops on its own.

questions.q: What are Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris?
o: The Italian and French names for the same grape
A white grape and a black grape
The dry and sweet versions of Pinot Noir
questions.ex: Pinot Grigio is the Italian name and Pinot Gris the French.

questions.q: Most Pinot Grigio is made from high yields picked early. What is the result?
o: Dry, light-bodied, high acidity, simple apple and lemon
Full-bodied, medium acidity, peach and mango
questions.ex: This is the common Italian style, best drunk young.

questions.q: Which describes a typical Alsace Pinot Gris?
o: Medium to full body, medium acidity, peach, mango and ginger, dry to medium
Light body, high acidity, simple apple and lemon, always dry
Light body, sweet, with pronounced herbaceous notes
Full body, high tannin, red fruit
questions.ex: In Alsace the grapes are picked extra-ripe. The best come from grand cru sites and can gain honey with age.

questions.q: Most inexpensive, high-volume Pinot Grigio comes from which Italian region, labelled delle Venezie DOC or Veneto IGT?
questions.ex: These wines are simple, unoaked, light and usually acceptable to good in quality.

questions.q: Where in Italy is a more complex, fuller-bodied Pinot Grigio made?
questions.ex: Friuli-Venezia Giulia is in north-east Italy's far corner.

questions.q: What does Vendanges tardives on an Alsace label mean?
o: Late harvest, usually a medium to sweet wine from extra-ripe grapes
The grapes were affected by noble rot
The wine was bottled at the estate
questions.ex: The term can only be used in Alsace. Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gewurztraminer can all be labelled VT.

questions.q: Which three grapes can make Alsace Grand Cru wines?
o: Chenin Blanc, Viognier and Pinot Gris
Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Sylvaner
questions.ex: Grand cru sites sit on steep east and south-east-facing slopes of the Vosges foothills.

questions.q: Outside Italy and France, what does a producer usually signal by calling the wine Pinot Grigio rather than Pinot Gris?
questions.ex: Pinot Gris signals a wine with more body and complexity.
